ox: Incorrect. Competition, urgency and hostility describe the TYPE A personality pattern, linked to heart disease, not hardiness.
Correct. Hardiness (Kobasa) = the three C's: Commitment, Control and Challenge. Hardy people stay involved, believe they can influence events, and see change as a chance to grow.
Incorrect. Denial, projection and repression are defense mechanisms (psychoanalytic), not traits that buffer stress in the hardiness model.
Incorrect. Alarm, resistance and exhaustion are Selye's three stages of the general adaptation syndrome, a description of stress, not a protective trait trio.

p: Hardiness was described by Kobasa as a set of three attitudes that buffer stress: Commitment (staying involved), Control (believing you can influence events) and Challenge (seeing change as an opportunity). Do not confuse it with Type A traits, defense mechanisms or Selye's GAS stages, which are also famous lists.

x6C_090.trap: Picking Type A traits or GAS stages because they are also famous trios.
mem: Type A = competitive, urgent, hostile → higher heart-disease risk.
x6C_090.sc: 'Trio that BUFFERS stress' = the positive three C's. Negative-sounding trios are distractors.
x6C_090.mn: CCC makes you tough: Commit, Control, Challenge.
x6C_090.plain: Hardy people think: 'I'm in this (commitment), I can steer it (control), and it's a chance to grow (challenge).'

ox: Problem-focused coping tries to change the stressor itself (make a plan, fix the problem). A loss cannot be undone, so this does not fit.
Correct. Meditation calms feelings when the situation cannot be changed. That is emotion-focused coping, and it is often a good, adaptive choice for uncontrollable stress.
The alarm stage is the body's first physiological reaction in Selye's model. It is a stage of stress, not something a person chooses to do to cope.
Learned helplessness is giving up because past stress seemed uncontrollable. Meditating to calm yourself is an active strategy, not passive giving up.

p: Coping is how we deal with stress. Problem-focused coping tackles the cause of stress. Emotion-focused coping manages the feelings the stress causes.
If the cause cannot be changed, such as a death, emotion-focused coping (meditation, talking, relaxing) is the fitting choice.

d_6C_14.trap: Thinking emotion-focused coping is always unhealthy avoidance. It is adaptive when the stressor cannot be changed.
d_6C_14.plain: If your ball rolls over a fence you can climb it (fix the problem). If your pet has passed away, you cannot fix it, so you comfort yourself.

ox: Safety, love, and esteem are levels of Maslow's hierarchy of needs. The trap is that both theories are about needs.
Drive, incentive, and arousal are separate theories of motivation (drive-reduction, incentive, arousal theory). They are not the three needs of self-determination theory.
Correct. Self-determination theory says people thrive and feel intrinsically motivated when they have autonomy (control), competence (skill), and relatedness (connection).
Extrinsic, intrinsic, and amotivation are TYPES of motivation. They describe what drives behavior, not the needs that must be met.

p: Self-determination theory says people are most motivated from the inside (intrinsic motivation) when three needs are met. Autonomy: feeling in control of your choices. Competence: feeling skilled. Relatedness: feeling connected to others.
Outside rewards (extrinsic motivation) can weaken inner motivation if they reduce autonomy.

mem: Maslow's levels are different (physiological, safety, love, esteem, self-actualization)
d_6C_23.trap: Confusing these three needs with Maslow's hierarchy levels or with types of motivation.
d_6C_23.plain: You love a video game more when you choose it yourself, you get good at it, and you play with friends.

ox: The opposite happens. The amygdala drives fear and aggression, so removing it lowers them. Assuming damage raises fear is the trap.
Vision is not lost. The animals see but fail to recognize what objects are (visual agnosia), so they treat things oddly.
The defining signs are emotional and behavioral (tameness, no fear, oral exploring). Memory deficits alone are linked more to hippocampal damage.
Correct. This is Klüver-Bucy syndrome: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality (putting things in the mouth), and hypersexuality.

p: The amygdala is a small almond-shaped brain structure that processes fear and aggression. It sits in the temporal lobe.

Removing both temporal lobes including the amygdala causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome. Animals become calm and fearless, put everything in their mouths (hyperorality), and show increased sexual behavior (hypersexuality).

mem: Klüver-Bucy: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality, hypersexuality
d_6C_40.trap: Assuming amygdala damage makes animals more fearful or aggressive. It makes them tame.
d_6C_40.plain: The amygdala is like the brain's smoke alarm. Remove it and the animal is no longer scared of anything, even things it should fear.

ox: Correct. The drug gave arousal, and the confederate's mood gave the cognitive label (happy or angry). Emotion = arousal + label from the situation. This is the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory.
James-Lange says each emotion comes from a specific pattern of body changes. It does not explain the same arousal becoming different emotions by context.
Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion happen at the same time and independently. It gives no role to context labeling the arousal.
Yerkes-Dodson says performance is best at moderate arousal. It is about performance, not which emotion is felt.

p: This theory says emotion needs two things: physical arousal and a cognitive label for it. We look at the situation to decide what the arousal means.
In the study, the same drug-caused arousal felt like happiness near a happy person and anger near an angry one.

mem: Cannon-Bard = body and emotion at the same time

r: Stimulus, arousal and emotion at the same time
Stimulus, arousal, label from context, emotion

q100.trap: Choosing James-Lange because arousal is involved. The key clue is that context changes the emotion for the same arousal.
q100.plain: Your heart pounds. If you are on a roller coaster you call it excitement. If you are in a dark alley you call it fear. Same body feeling, different label.

ox: Correct. Selye's general adaptation syndrome: alarm (fight-or-flight activation), resistance (body stays on high alert and copes), exhaustion (resources run out, illness risk).
Resistance cannot come first. The body must first react to the stressor (alarm) before it can sustain a response.
Appraisal and coping belong to cognitive models like Lazarus and Folkman, not Selye's physiological model.
Exhaustion is the last stage, after prolonged stress has drained the body. Putting it first reverses the order.

p: Hans Selye described how the body responds to ongoing stress in three stages. Alarm: the sympathetic nervous system fires up (fight-or-flight). Resistance: the body stays alert and tries to cope. Exhaustion: energy is depleted and illness becomes more likely.

q101.mn: A-R-E: Alarm, Resistance, Exhaustion ('Are you stressed?').
q101.trap: Scrambling the order. Remember that you must react (alarm) first and run out of energy (exhaustion) last.
q101.plain: Like a runner. First the starting burst (alarm), then keeping up the pace (resistance), then collapsing at the end of a too-long race (exhaustion).

ox: Sensory, perceptual, and motor describe taking in and acting on stimuli. They are not the parts of an emotional experience.
Conscious, preconscious, and unconscious are Freud's levels of awareness. They say nothing about how emotion is built.
Correct. Emotion has a physiological part (heart rate, sweating), a cognitive part (appraisal and feeling), and a behavioral part (expressions and actions).

Primary and secondary are used to describe appraisal (primary appraisal: is this relevant to me; secondary: can I cope) and reinforcers (primary: innately rewarding; secondary: learned). They are not a standard three-part list, and none of them are the parts of an emotion.

p: Psychologists say an emotion has three parts. Physiological: body changes like a racing heart. Cognitive: your thoughts and the feeling you have about the situation. Behavioral: what you show or do, like smiling or running away.

x6C_001.trap: Picking Freud's three levels of awareness because they also come in threes.
x6C_001.plain: When you are scared: your tummy drops (body), you think 'that is a big dog' (thinking), and you run (action).

ox: Cognitive is the internal appraisal and feeling. You cannot see it directly, but a smile or fist can be seen.
Physiological means internal body responses such as heart rate and sweating. Facial and muscle actions are outward expressions, so this is the confusing near-miss.
Perception is interpreting sensory input. It is not an emotion component.
Correct. Smiling, frowning, and clenching fists are observable expressions and actions, which make up the behavioral component.

p: The behavioral component is the visible part of emotion: facial expressions, posture, gestures, and actions. Other people can observe it directly.
The physiological component is internal and automatic, like heart rate, blood pressure, and sweating.

x6C_003.trap: Calling facial muscle movements physiological. Muscle movements you can see are behavioral.
x6C_003.plain: Behavior is what a camera can film. Physiology is what only a doctor's machine can measure.

ox: If people had learned the expressions by modeling, they would need exposure to Western faces. The community had none, so this does not explain the finding.
Display rules are learned norms about when to show emotions, and they differ across cultures. This study is about recognition, not display norms.

The study tests whether expressions are recognized across cultures, not the order of arousal and labeling. Arousal followed by a cognitive label is the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory. Do not confuse a theory of timing with a finding about universality.
Correct. Accurate matching without cultural contact suggests some expressions (like fear and anger) are inborn and shared by all humans.

p: Researchers like Ekman found that people across cultures recognize basic emotions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger, disgust, surprise) in faces. This holds even for isolated groups with no media exposure.
That suggests basic expressions are biologically built in. What differs by culture is display rules, the norms for when to show them.

mem: Isolated groups with no media still recognize them
x6C_006.trap: Choosing observational learning. No exposure means nothing to copy from.
x6C_006.plain: A baby anywhere in the world cries when hurt. You do not need to be taught that sound, so it must be built in.

ox: Correct. Display rules are culturally learned norms about when, where, and how strongly to show emotion. Hiding grief in public but weeping in private is a display rule.
The facial feedback hypothesis says expressions change how we feel. It does not address social norms controlling expression.
The private weeping shows grief is felt. Only public display is controlled, so this does not show a lack of universal emotions.
Cannon-Bard is about arousal and feeling happening at the same time. It does not explain cultural norms.

p: Display rules are learned cultural norms about showing emotion. They tell you which emotions to show, to whom, and how strongly.
The emotion itself is still felt. Only the outward expression is managed.

mem: The emotion is felt; the expression is controlled
x6C_007.trap: Concluding that hidden expression means the emotion is absent. It is only masked in public.
x6C_007.plain: You may feel bored in class, but you do not make a bored face at the teacher. You hide it because of the rules.

ox: Darwin stressed inheritance and evolution. Learning from caregivers would not explain similar expressions across species.
Appraisal theories came much later and do not explain why animals and humans share expressions.
Correct. Darwin proposed that expressions evolved as adaptive signals, such as showing threat or submission, that helped survival.
Conditioning is a behaviorist idea about learned reward associations. It is not Darwin's argument.

concept.t: Darwin and the evolution of emotion
p: Darwin argued that emotional expressions are inherited, like physical traits. They evolved because they helped communication and survival, such as warning others of danger or showing you are not a threat.
This predicts expressions are similar across humans and other animals.

mem: Darwin: expressions are evolved and inherited
x6C_008.trap: Picking a learning explanation. Similarity across species points to evolution, not experience.
x6C_008.plain: A dog bares its teeth to say 'back off.' That warning saved fights, so it stuck around over generations.

ox: Two-factor theory needs arousal plus a cognitive label. The pen task only changed facial muscles, so it does not test this.
Cannon-Bard says emotion is not caused by body changes. This result (face changing feeling) goes against it.
Yerkes-Dodson links arousal level to performance. Nothing here is about performance.
Correct. Facial feedback hypothesis: the position of facial muscles sends signals back that influence how strongly you feel an emotion. Forced smiling made cartoons seem funnier.

p: This idea says your facial expression can shape your feelings. Smiling can make you feel happier, and frowning can make you feel worse.
In the pen study, holding a pen in the teeth forces a smile shape. Holding it in the lips blocks one. Smilers rated cartoons funnier. Note: some large replications gave mixed results.

mem: A version of body-influences-emotion, like James-Lange
x6C_009.trap: Choosing Schachter-Singer because it is a famous emotion theory. Here only facial muscles were changed.
x6C_009.plain: Pretending to smile in a mirror can sometimes trick your mood into brightening.

ox: Universality is about recognizing expressions across cultures. This lab result about being filmed does not address it.
One moderator weakening an effect does not prove emotion is fully set by cognitive labels.
Correct. A moderator is a variable that changes an effect's strength. Being filmed likely raises self-awareness, which interferes with facial feedback. It does not prove the effect is fake.
Timing of arousal and emotion was not measured, so this does not support simultaneity (Cannon-Bard).

p: A moderator is a variable that changes how strong an effect is. Here, being filmed shrinks the facial feedback effect.
A reasonable reading is that self-awareness disrupts the link between facial muscles and feelings. Do not over-conclude: one moderator does not show the effect never exists.

mem: Moderator = changes the strength of an effect
Choose the conclusion the data actually support
Avoid sweeping claims from one finding
x6C_010.trap: Over-generalizing, such as 'emotion is entirely cognitive'. The data only show a condition that weakens the effect.
x6C_010.plain: A magic trick may work when nobody watches, but fail when everyone stares and you get nervous. Being watched changed the result.

ox: Correct. James-Lange says emotion is the perception of bodily changes. Less bodily feedback should then mean weaker emotion, which matches the finding.
Cannon-Bard says feeling and body arousal are independent. It predicts spinal injury would not change emotion intensity.
Lazarus's appraisal theory stresses thinking about the situation, not the amount of bodily feedback.
Opponent-process theory is about emotional rebound after a stimulus fades, not bodily feedback.

p: James-Lange says you feel an emotion because you sense your body's reaction. First the body responds, then you feel the emotion.
So if bodily feedback is reduced, as in a high spinal cord injury, the emotion should feel weaker. Real data on this are mixed, so this is a test of the prediction.

mem: James-Lange: body change first, then emotion
Less bodily feedback predicts weaker emotion
x6C_013.trap: Choosing Cannon-Bard. It says emotion does not depend on body feedback, so it predicts no change.
x6C_013.plain: You feel scared because you notice your heart pounding. If you could not feel your heart or hands shaking, the fear would feel smaller.

ox: Wrong. This shows arousal alone is nonspecific, which is a different Cannon point. It says nothing about how fast body changes happen compared with feelings. Trap: right theory, wrong objection.
Wrong. Cross-cultural faces speak to whether emotions are universal and innate. They do not compare timing of body changes and feelings.
Correct. If people feel fear before sweating or a racing heart begins, the body change cannot be the cause of the feeling. That directly supports Cannon's timing objection.
Wrong. Appraisal findings support Lazarus-type theories. They do not test whether body changes are too slow.

p: James-Lange says the body reacts first, and the feeling is just our awareness of that reaction. Cannon disagreed with this idea.
One of his points was timing. Body (visceral) changes like sweating are slow, taking seconds. Emotions can appear almost instantly. A cause cannot come after its effect.

mem: Cannon's objections: body changes are too slow, arousal is nonspecific, and people without body feedback still feel emotion.
Timing evidence = feeling comes BEFORE the body change.
Nonspecific arousal evidence = epinephrine gives arousal with no particular emotion.
x6C_015.sc: Match the finding to the objection. Words like 'before' or 'too slow' point to timing.
x6C_015.trap: Picking the epinephrine answer because it is also anti-James-Lange. It supports a different objection from the one asked.
x6C_015.plain: If the smoke alarm only rang after you already smelled smoke, the alarm could not be how you found out about the fire.

ox: Wrong. Both groups got the arousing injection, so both were aroused. Trap: thinking the difference is in the body rather than the explanation.
Correct. The informed group had an obvious nonemotional cause for the racing heart, the injection. They did not label it as anger at the confederate.
Wrong. The thalamus is part of Cannon-Bard theory and is not the explanation here. No blocking of cortex was shown.
Wrong. Coping strategies were not measured. Nobody removed the confederate. The groups differed in how they explained their arousal.

p: Two-factor theory says emotion needs two parts: physical arousal and a mental label for why you are aroused.
If you already have an explanation for the arousal, such as a drug, you do not need an emotional label. If you have no explanation, you look to the situation and label it with an emotion, like anger.

mem: Informed about the arousal cause = less emotion.
Uninformed = copies the mood of the situation or confederate.
x6C_017.trap: Saying the informed group had no arousal. The arousal was the same. The label was different.
x6C_017.plain: If your stomach growls and you know you skipped lunch, you are not worried. If you have no idea why, you might think something is wrong.

ox: Correct. Fear arousal from the bridge was mislabeled as attraction to the interviewer. This is the classic misattribution of arousal, a two-factor theory idea.
Wrong. Mere exposure means liking something more from repeated contact. Contact time was about the same on both bridges, so it cannot explain the difference.
Wrong. Facial feedback says facial muscles shape emotion. No facial expressions were manipulated here.
Wrong. Habituation means a response gets weaker with repeated exposure. Here the arousal was used to create attraction, not weakened.

p: Misattribution means you feel aroused for one reason but give the credit to another. This is a main prediction of two-factor theory.
On the shaky bridge, men felt a racing heart from fear. An attractive person was nearby, so some labeled the arousal as attraction.

mem: Dutton and Aron suspension bridge study = misattribution of arousal.
Arousal from one source gets credited to another cue.
x6C_018.trap: Choosing mere exposure because the men met the researcher. Both groups met her equally.
x6C_018.plain: You run hard, then a friend smiles at you, and your pounding heart feels like a crush even though it was the running.

ox: Wrong. James-Lange starts with the body response and gives the feeling afterward. It does not explain why the same snake leads to different feelings. Trap: forgetting that the appraisal comes before the body response.
Wrong. Cannon-Bard says feeling and arousal happen at once. It does not say why two people differ on identical input.
Correct. Lazarus says emotion depends on how you judge, or appraise, a situation. A harmless snake means calm. A venomous snake means terror.
Wrong. Facial feedback needs a facial expression to drive emotion. Nothing about faces is in the question.

p: Appraisal is your quick mental judgment of whether something is dangerous or safe for you.
Lazarus says this judgment comes first. It decides both the emotion and the body response. So the same event can cause different emotions in different people.

mem: Lazarus: appraisal comes first, then emotion.
Schachter-Singer needs arousal first. Lazarus does not.
x6C_020.trap: Choosing James-Lange because it is the first theory you learned. Look for the clue that interpretation drives emotion.
x6C_020.plain: Two kids hear a dog bark. One thinks the dog is friendly and smiles. The other thinks it will bite and cries.

ox: Wrong. This is the classic Schachter-Singer result, in which unexplained arousal is labeled using the situation. It does not separate the two theories in favor of Lazarus.
Wrong. Weaker emotions after spinal injury would support James-Lange, which depends on body feedback.
Correct. If emotion follows appraisal while arousal is fixed and explained, labeling of unexplained arousal is not needed. That favors Lazarus.
Wrong. Arousal and feeling at the same moment supports Cannon-Bard.

p: Schachter-Singer says emotion = arousal plus a label for unexplained arousal. Arousal is required.
Lazarus says emotion follows your appraisal of the situation, and arousal is a consequence. So holding arousal constant and still changing emotion with appraisal favors Lazarus.

mem: Appraisal changes emotion with arousal held constant = Lazarus.
x6C_021.trap: Picking the confederate answer because it is the most famous experiment. It supports the other theory.
x6C_021.plain: One theory says you need a loud noise before you decide how to feel. The other says your thoughts about the noise decide, even if the noise stays the same.

ox: Wrong. Schachter-Singer is about arousal plus a cognitive label. It has no thalamic relay.
Correct. In Cannon-Bard, the thalamus sends signals at the same time to the cortex for the feeling and to the autonomic system for the body response.
Wrong. James-Lange says feeling comes from feedback about body changes, so the body reaction comes first.
Wrong. Lazarus emphasizes cortical appraisal, not a thalamic relay.

p: Cannon-Bard says the feeling of emotion and the body response happen at the same time and independently.
The thalamus is a relay station in the brain. A stimulus reaches it, and it sends one signal to the cortex (the conscious feeling) and another to the body (arousal).

mem: Cannon-Bard is called the thalamic theory.
x6C_024.trap: Mixing up Cannon-Bard and James-Lange. Think 'Cannon = Concurrent' (same time).
x6C_024.mn: Cannon = Concurrent: both happen at once.
x6C_024.plain: A mail room clerk gets one letter and sends a copy to two offices at the same moment.

ox: Correct. The amygdala supports the conditioned emotional response. The hippocampus supports explicit memory of the pairing. Each patient lost a different one.
Wrong. Each patient kept one kind of learning, so neither structure is needed for all fear learning. Trap: not reading what each patient kept.
Wrong. The hippocampal patient still had the skin-conductance response, so the hippocampus is not needed for it.
Wrong. Nothing in the case involves the cerebellum. The damage was to the hippocampus and amygdala.

p: A double dissociation is when damage to structure A harms function 1 but not 2, and damage to B harms function 2 but not 1. It shows the two functions use different structures.
Here, amygdala damage removes the conditioned fear response. Hippocampal damage removes explicit knowledge of the pairing.

mem: Double dissociation = two structures, two functions.
x6C_028.trap: Assuming both regions are needed for everything. The patients show the opposite.
x6C_028.plain: Two light switches run two lamps. Break switch A and only lamp 1 dies. Break switch B and only lamp 2 dies. So each switch runs its own lamp.

ox: Correct. Klüver-Bucy follows bilateral anterior temporal damage including the amygdala. It causes tameness, hyperorality and reduced fear.
Wrong. Korsakoff syndrome is a memory disorder from thiamine deficiency, often in alcohol use. It does not cause fearless tameness.
Wrong. Wernicke aphasia is a language comprehension problem from damage to Wernicke's area. It is not a fear or oral exploration disorder.
Wrong. Learned helplessness is passivity after uncontrollable stress. It is learned, not caused by a lesion.

p: Klüver-Bucy syndrome happens after damage to both temporal lobes, including the amygdala.
The amygdala helps judge threat. Without it, animals lose fear and become tame. They also put objects in their mouths (hyperorality).

mem: Bilateral amygdala and temporal lobe damage: tame, fearless, hyperoral.
x6C_029.trap: Confusing Klüver-Bucy with Korsakoff because both start with K. Korsakoff is memory loss.
x6C_029.plain: A guard dog that no longer cares about strangers and chews on everything.

ox: Wrong. Rage still appeared with the cortex removed, so the cortex is not needed to produce it. Trap: reversing cause and control.
Wrong. The hippocampus was not what the experiment isolated. It is mainly tied to memory.
Correct. The intact hypothalamus produced rage without cortex. The poor aim and lack of restraint show the cortex normally directs and inhibits it.
Wrong. Labeling needs cortical processing, and the cats had no cortex yet still showed rage.

p: Sham rage is sudden, poorly aimed anger. It appeared in cats with the cortex removed but the hypothalamus intact.
So the hypothalamus can generate the rage pattern. The cortex normally acts like a brake, controlling and directing the behavior.

mem: Sham rage = rage with no cortex.
x6C_033.trap: Thinking the cortex produces emotion. The cats show it controls emotion instead.
x6C_033.plain: A car with a working engine but no driver. It lurches forward, but nobody steers or brakes.

Wrong. Amygdala activity fell during reappraisal, so it is not driving the process. Trap: reading the direction backward.
Wrong. Amygdala activity changed, so emotional processing was affected.
Wrong. fMRI is correlational. It cannot prove one structure causes all emotions. The word 'all' is a red flag.

p: Reappraisal means rethinking a situation to change how it makes you feel, such as telling yourself an image is staged.
The prefrontal cortex handles planning and control. The amygdala handles threat and fear. More prefrontal activity with less amygdala activity suggests top-down control.

mem: Prefrontal cortex can down-regulate the amygdala.
fMRI shows correlation, not proof of causation.

x6C_034.plain: Your thinking brain tells your alarm brain, 'It is just a movie,' and the alarm quiets down.

Wrong. The hippocampus was not tested, and it is known to be involved in memory.
Wrong. Cortisol was not manipulated, so the study says nothing about it.

p: Consolidation means turning a new memory into a lasting one. After a scary event, norepinephrine acts on beta-adrenergic receptors, especially in the amygdala, to strengthen it.
A beta-blocker blocks those receptors. Giving one right after training weakens the memory.

mem: Norepinephrine on beta receptors boosts consolidation of emotional memory.
Beta-blockers given after learning weaken it.

x6C_036.plain: Strong feelings act like a highlighter on a memory. A beta-blocker takes the highlighter away.

Correct. The low road goes from thalamus straight to amygdala, skipping the sensory cortex. It is fast but crude.
Wrong. This is not a fear pathway LeDoux described.
Wrong. The retina to hypothalamus path mostly helps set circadian rhythm, not fear.

concept.t: LeDoux's low road and high road
p: The low road sends sensory information from the thalamus straight to the amygdala. It is fast but gives only rough detail.
The high road goes thalamus to sensory cortex to amygdala. It is slower but more accurate, and can cancel a false alarm.

mem: Low road: thalamus to amygdala, fast, crude.
High road: thalamus to cortex to amygdala, slow, detailed.
Low road works before conscious thought.
x6C_037.trap: Mixing up which route skips the cortex. Low means a shortcut.
x6C_037.plain: You jump at a curled stick that looks like a snake, then look closer and relax.

Wrong. The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle and is not part of the autonomic system.
Wrong. The enteric system runs the gut and does not drive fight-or-flight.
Correct. The sympathetic division prepares the body for action with a faster heart rate, dilated pupils and bronchioles, and energy release.

p: The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary body functions. It has two main divisions that work in opposite ways.
Sympathetic means fight or flight: it speeds up the heart and releases energy. Parasympathetic means rest and digest: it slows the heart and boosts digestion.

Rest and digest: heart slower, digestion up

x6C_042.plain: Every relay runner hands off the first baton the same way. Only the last handoff differs.

concept.t: Correlation vs causation in stress research
p: The Social Readjustment Rating Scale adds up points for life changes, both good and bad, as a measure of stress.

x6C_057.trap: Choosing a causal answer. On the MCAT, correlational design means choose the 'associated with' wording.
x6C_057.plain: Ice cream sales and sunburns go up together, but ice cream does not cause sunburn. Summer does.

ox: Correct. One goal (the job) has both a good side (high pay) and a bad side (long commute). Wanting and dreading the same thing is approach-avoidance.
Approach-approach means choosing between two good options. She has only one job, and it has a downside.
Avoidance-avoidance means being stuck between two bad options. She actually wants the job, so this does not fit.
A catastrophic stressor is a huge event like a flood or war. A job decision is a personal, everyday stressor.

p: A conflict is feeling pulled in two directions. In an approach-avoidance conflict, one goal has both attractive and unattractive features.
As you get closer to the goal, the urge to avoid usually grows faster than the urge to approach, so anxiety rises.

mem: Approach-avoidance: one goal, good AND bad.
Avoidance grows faster as you get closer.
x6C_061.sc: Ask: how many options are there? One option with mixed feelings equals approach-avoidance.
x6C_061.trap: Count the goals. One goal with pros and cons is approach-avoidance. Two separate goals means approach-approach or avoidance-avoidance.
x6C_061.plain: It is like wanting to eat a huge ice cream cone, but it is so cold it hurts your teeth. One thing, two feelings.

ox: Correct. Stress was only measured, not assigned. People with high stress may also sleep less, smoke more, or eat worse. Those other variables (confounds) could explain the cold risk.
Giving everyone the same virus is a strength because it controls exposure. It does not make the study correlational.
Every study has a dependent variable (the outcome). Having one does not block causal claims.
This is false. Cold resistance depends on immune function, and that is why stress could matter.

p: To show cause, researchers must manipulate the independent variable (the thing they change) and randomly assign people to groups.
Here, stress was just measured. A confound is an outside factor, like poor sleep, that could affect both stress and illness.

mem: Causation needs manipulation plus random assignment.
A confound is a hidden third variable.
x6C_066.trap: Students pick an answer praising a design feature (same virus). The real issue is that stress was not randomly assigned.
x6C_066.plain: If kids with more screen time get lower grades, maybe a third thing, like less sleep, causes both.

ox: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination. It is not the main target of stress hormones affecting memory.
The primary visual cortex processes what you see, not memory. Do not pick it because it sounds like a brain part you know.
The pons relays signals and helps with sleep and breathing. It is not a major cortisol target for memory.
Correct. The hippocampus has many glucocorticoid (cortisol) receptors. Long-term high cortisol can damage its neurons and shrink it, hurting memory.

p: Cortisol is a stress hormone made by the adrenal glands. The hippocampus is a brain region that forms new memories.
The hippocampus has many cortisol receptors. Too much cortisol for too long can harm it, so memory gets worse.

mem: Amygdala handles fear and emotion; it can grow under stress.
x6C_067.trap: Mixing up the hippocampus with the amygdala. Hippocampus equals memory; amygdala equals fear.
x6C_067.plain: Think of a memory-making machine that is very sensitive to heat. Constant stress overheats it, so it stops saving files well.

ox: Selye's model is built on physiological changes like hormones and organ effects. It does not lack them.
Selye said the opposite: prolonged stress wears the body down and causes illness.
The General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) was proposed for stressors in general, bad or good.
Correct. Selye described one uniform body response to any stressor. Lazarus and others showed that how you appraise (judge) the event changes your response.

p: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome has three stages: alarm, resistance, exhaustion. He said the body responds the same way to any stressor.
Critics say this ignores appraisal, which is how a person judges a threat. Control and predictability change the response.

x6C_073.mn: Selye stages: A-R-E, where A = Alarm, R = Resistance, E = Exhaustion.
x6C_073.trap: Thinking the critique is about missing biology. It is about missing psychology.
x6C_073.plain: Two kids get the same pop quiz. One panics and one shrugs. Selye said they react the same, but they do not.

ox: Intensity was the same in both groups, yet ulcers differed. So intensity is not the only factor.
The warned rats had fewer ulcers, so the tone did not make stress worse. A warning helps.
Correct. Shocks were equal. Only predictability differed, and unpredictable shocks caused more ulcers. Predictability reduces harm.
The study only shows that stress features change ulcer rates. It does not say bacteria never cause ulcers, and that claim is not drawn from this design.

p: Stress harm depends on more than how strong the stressor is. It also depends on how predictable it is.
A warning signal tells the animal when it is safe, so it can relax between shocks. Without a warning, the body stays on alert.

mem: Same physical stressor, different psychological features.
x6C_074.trap: Picking a choice that ignores the design. Same shocks means the difference comes from the one thing that changed.
x6C_074.plain: A fire drill with a bell is easier than a surprise alarm at any moment. You can relax when there is no bell.

ox: Both rats received exactly the same shocks. Yoked designs exist to make shock amount equal.
Correct. Shock was identical. Only one rat could control it. The rat without control got sicker, so perceived control matters.
Exercise could be a confound, but the design is built to test control, and control is the intended finding.
Roles are assigned randomly, so genetics should be spread evenly. It is not the key variable.

p: In a yoked design, two animals get the same stressor. Only one can control it, for example by turning a wheel.
The animal without control gets sicker. This shows that having control, or feeling you have it, reduces stress harm.

mem: Control over a stressor lowers harm.
Lack of control relates to learned helplessness.
x6C_075.trap: Picking total shock. In a yoked design that is held equal on purpose.
x6C_075.plain: Two kids ride the same bumpy bus. One can pull the brake and the other cannot. The one without the brake feels worse.

ox: Cortisol being objective is good measurement, but measurement alone cannot prove cause.
Using only stressed employees affects who the results apply to (generalizability), not whether cause is shown.
Length of study does not create causation. Many long studies are still correlational.
Correct. Random assignment makes the groups about equal on motivation, health, and baseline stress. Only the meditation differs, so the cortisol difference can be credited to it.

p: Random assignment means chance decides who goes to which group. This spreads out hidden differences evenly.
If groups start equal and only one gets the treatment, a later difference is likely caused by the treatment.

mem: Waitlist group acts as the control.
x6C_086.trap: Mixing up random assignment (cause) with random sampling (who the results apply to).
x6C_086.plain: Picking teams by drawing names from a hat keeps strong players from landing on only one team.

ox: Correct. Cognitive restructuring changes how threatening the interview seems. That is a change in appraisal.
The interview still happens. Only the thought about it changes, not the stressor.
The parasympathetic system (the calming branch) may calm down afterward, but the therapist is not controlling it directly. The new thought leads to that effect.
An external locus of control means believing outside forces run your life. That would raise stress, and it is not what the therapist is teaching.

p: Appraisal is how you judge a situation: threat or challenge. Cognitive restructuring replaces extreme thoughts with realistic ones.
Because the situation seems less threatening, arousal drops. The thought changed first.

mem: Catastrophizing is an extreme negative thought.
x6C_092.trap: Choosing the stressor itself. A thought-based method changes the view of the stressor, not the stressor.
x6C_092.plain: If you think the dog barking is a monster, you are scared. Learn it is a puppy and you relax. The dog did not change, your thought did.

ox: The theory says the felt initial reaction gets weaker with repetition, not stronger.
This describes the two-factor theory (arousal plus a label). It is not opponent-process.
Correct. The opposing process grows stronger with repetition and cancels more of the initial reaction. Terror fades and elation grows.
The sympathetic system still responds. What shifts is the emotional balance, not whether arousal happens.

p: Opponent-process theory says every strong emotion triggers an opposite emotion afterward. The first process is the main feeling. The second is the opposite.
With repetition, the opposing process gets stronger. So the net initial feeling weakens and the opposite after-feeling grows.

x6C_094.trap: Thinking the initial emotion gets stronger. It is the opponent that grows.
x6C_094.plain: A seesaw: with practice, the opposite side gets heavier, so the first side hardly lifts.

ox: Group A still had arousal. It was reinterpreted, not removed.
The GAS stages are not skipped because someone is given instructions.
Correct. Group A was told arousal helps, so they reappraised it. A threat response shifted toward a challenge response, giving better heart efficiency and performance.
Nothing in the study taught Group B any coping method. They simply got no instructions.

p: A threat response happens when you feel the demands are bigger than your resources. A challenge response happens when you feel you can handle it.
Reinterpreting arousal as helpful moves you toward challenge, with more efficient heart function and better performance.

mem: Reappraisal changes the meaning of arousal.
Challenge: better performance and heart efficiency.
x6C_097.trap: Thinking arousal vanished. It was still there, just seen differently.
x6C_097.plain: Butterflies before a game can mean you are scared or you are ready. Calling it ready helps you play better.
